items.title: Claude can now turn artifacts into semi-independent Mac apps
items.content_html:
While a new Claude feature makes it seem like making a Mac app is now easier than ever, a major caveat means these AI-generated apps are worth avoiding altogether.

While Apple itself has recognized the potential of AI-assisted software development, with Xcode 27 adding support for agentic coding, other companies have taken things further. Rather than an AI agent suggesting user interface layouts, Anthropic's Claude can now build macOS apps from prompts.

In a press release on the Claude website, Anthropic revealed that its users can now "use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps." Dubbed the "Install as app" feature, the capability is rolling out in beta for Claude users running macOS and Windows.

As for how this will work in practice, Anthropic's video suggests that making Mac apps with Claude is a straightforward endeavor. With a single prompt asking Claude to make a tool, and a click of a button thereafter, Anthropic's virtual assistant will generate a Mac app on the fly.

Anthropic emphasizes that the apps generated by Claude have their own app icons, and that they open in dedicated windows, rather than in the Claude desktop app. Applications made by Claude can also add Menu Bar items and send notifications, among other things.

These AI-created apps are also capable of using Claude and associated connectors. However, Anthropic warns that "requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan's usage limits."

Buried at the very bottom of the webpage is a line that outlines a major caveat, however. "You need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app."

Given that desktop applications are often designed to work without a Wi-Fi connection, this means anything made by Claude will automatically be inferior to existing third-party apps and solutions.

In short, no Wi-Fi and no Claude means you can't use your AI-generated app, even if you've already built and configured it. Massive limitation aside, Claude's app generation features do appear promising.

What sort of apps can you make with Claude?

The underlying technology behind these AI-generated applications is Claude artifacts. "Artifacts started out as a work output you'd share, like a chart or a webpage," says Anthropic, adding that people use Claude artifacts for everyday tasks.

"If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention." However, Claude can now make much more than charts and webpages.

Among other things, Anthropic says Claude was used to make a file manager, a full layered image editor, a terminal app, and a Menu Bar application. Simply put, the possibilities look endless.

Additionally, Anthropic says users can share Claude-created apps with others. The company has implemented a permission system, which lets users choose how the apps can interact with their Mac.

Claude app permissions

Applications created with Claude can be configured with three different permission settings:

  • Default - apps cannot do anything more than they would be able to within a web browser
  • App permissions - apps can request to access features that Claude controls, such as making always-on-top windows, listening for global shortcuts, and sending notifications.
  • Full computer access - apps can request to run programs and read, change, or delete the user's files without asking each time.

"You can only give full access to apps you made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by people in your organization," says Anthropic. The company warns that it "doesn't review apps before you install them," so it encourages its users to only give full access to trusted applications.

Claude's app generation feature is currently available in beta on all plans. We don't see a reason to use it, as you're better off sticking with third-party apps or using Xcode to build your own with AI agents.

items.title: National security, more affairs, and possible treason - Nvidia's problems are far from over
items.content_html:
Reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO is only the latest controversy surrounding Nvidia. It has not repaired Nvidia's reputational damage, and federal investigations that could see jail time will stretch on for years.

Trump said publicly that Jensen Huang did nothing wrong, and it was his intervention that made the Nvidia board reinstate the disgraced CEO despite its preference not to. However, two new reports detail just what Trump really felt, and precisely how Nvidia will remain in trouble.

"The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now [borne] by the board of Nvidia," Sen. Kevin Cramer (R., N.D.) has told the Wall Street Journal, "but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens."

Despite Trump even using the word "exonerated" about Jensen Huang, the new report confirms that the Department of Justice is still leading two investigations into Nvidia customers about chip smuggling to China. Then UPI reports that one of the firms, Megaspeed, has been blacklisted by the US Commerce Department.

This means that no US firm can trade with Megaspeed without special authorization. Megaspeed will not be able to buy from the US without a license, said the department, because it and related entities were "acting contrary to the national interest or foreign policy interests of the United States."

Megaspeed has previously claimed to have entirely complied with US export rules. It has said that Alice Huang, suspected of being a Chinese spy, has not worked at Megaspeed since August 2025. However, the US investigations include activity spanning back to 2024.

Trump is said to have not even heard of Jensen Huang until recently despite having hosted him for many White House tech briefings, but he has at least twice been briefed about Alice Huang (no familial relation). That includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefing him about intelligence concerns in May 2026.

However, Trump dismissed this and allowed the Nvidia CEO on his trip to China.

What prompted the pressure on Nvidia

Trump's move was prompted in part by vice president JD Vance's background as a former venture capitalist. According to unspecified officials, Vance saw Huang as critical in the US race against China's technology sector.

As Vance and Trump pressed the board, Nvidia's directors had a marathon session with Huang on Sunday, November 22. He reported disclosed yet more affairs than had been previously confirmed, but is said to have been contrite.

Chair Harvey Jones had previously stated that Huang had previously exhibited "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms."

On November 23, Jones changed his tone.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia," he said, "and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

It's perhaps unsurprising that he listed stockholders first. But if both the board and Trump believed that reinstating Huang would restore the company's fortunes, they may not have been right for very long.

Since Jensen Huang was reinstated, with immediate effect, Nvidia saw the largest-ever one-day market cap it has seen. After falling by more than $1 trillion, the stock gained almost $800 billion, in the span of just a few hours.

Consequently Trump said that "the response from the market has been very positive... that really shows the decision was right."

On Tuesday, the investors disagreed, at least in part. As of 1:30 PM ET on November 24, the stock bled off about 1/3 of the gains of the previous day, falling a bit more than 7.1% in an extremely busy trading day for the company.

What happens next

Trump asserted that Jensen Huang didn't do anything illegal, he just "made some indiscretions having to do with other things." He was able to say this because Attorney General Todd Blanche reported that Huang himself wasn't the subject of any Justice Department investigation.

The implication is that if Nvidia was complicit in illegal activities, its CEO knew nothing about it. That doesn't fit the image of a CEO who is an irreplaceable genius.

"If we didn't do this," said Trump, "I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, 'Hey, how would you like to come to China?'"

There are investigations in California about the trade ban breaks. California's probe examines whether Nvidia illegally sold advanced chips to China or shared confidential information, and both claims certainly involve Jensen Huang. The subpoena issued by California is seeking information on potential civil and criminal violations under California state laws, including corporate securities rules.

It's not clear what Huang will be able to provide in his forthcoming testimony before Congress, and fifth amendment rights are expected to be asserted. That hearing is expected to be held, and live-streamed, on December 3, 2026.

During this same week, Nvidia is hosting a conference in Washington, DC, showcasing its technology. The odds are that, for the moment, it will be business as usual for Nvidia.

However, there is bipartisan criticism of Nvidia and it's unlikely that either Republicans or Democrats will let the controversy slide. Not when aiding and abetting a trade ban entails committing multiple felonies on the light penalty side, and is treason by code.

Where AppleInsider stands on the matter

We here at AppleInsider believe that a strong Nvidia is good for the US. Huang's lack of a succession plan is not a sign of a good CEO. Poor decision making in the man's personal life isn't the real issue, but it is a symptom of a larger one.

The White House has been clear that Nvidia chips in Chinese hands, whether professional or governmental, is a giant security risk. Under Huang's control, not even including if he facilitated the sale, extremely large quantities got there anyway. Accountability is important, and Huang is clear that he has none.

With two of us having served in sensitive positions in the US Navy, we are not fans of big tech moves that potentially endanger national security. This is the definition of that, assuming you listen to what the White House has said, and not the spin after the fact.

Nvidia can be strong. It doesn't need Huang to be that.

Ultimately, this tale will be told over years, not days or even months. And, like we've said, we're sure there's a lot more drama to come.

items.title: XNULinux can run macOS apps in Linux without a virtual machine
items.content_html: The XNULinux project is able to run macOS 27 and macOS apps on a Linux PC, all without requiring any virtualization. It's still not bootable, though.

items.title: XNULinux can run macOS apps in Linux without a virtual machine
items.content_html:
The XNULinux project is able to run macOS 27 and macOS apps on a Linux PC, all without requiring any virtualization. It's still not bootable, though.

Most Linux projects AppleInsider writes about involve trying to run Linux on a Mac. However, there's now a project that is running macOS on Linux.

Outside of building a Hackintosh, the usual way to run a macOS app on Linux or non-Apple hardware is through a virtual machine. However, that often introduces performance overheads that can impact the overall experience.

The XNULinux project sidesteps that issue by being able to run macOS 27 itself, without needing modifications. Since macOS can run, apps running within macOS 27 can also run on the Linux computer.

So far, it can run macOS 27.2.1, complete with a working desktop and Dock, and can run various apps including Spotlight, Safari, Notes, and Calculator.

Kernels in kernels

The project works by loading the macOS kernel into the Linux kernel, so that macOS runs directly within Linux. It uses XNU, the open-source kernel used for macOS published by Apple, and inserts it as a loadable kernel module within an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel.

That hosted XNU kernel is able to run the CPU and memory management unit (MMU) directly. In effect, macOS processes can run natively alongside Linux processes through the same CPU without any hypervisor.

XNU gets memory, timers, files, network, and GPU access from Linux via a small interface module.

As it stands, the project is in its early days, and has been tested on a few hardware configurations. This has included an Nvidia DGX Spark running on bare metal.

A Terminal screen accessing macOS normally [left], and a Terminal with an SSH session into the Linux version that macOS is running inside [right], running on an Nvidia DGX Spark - Image Credit: XNULinux

A second setup has been running on an arm64 Linux virtual machine on an Apple Silicon Mac. This is effectively macOS running on a Linux in a virtual machine running on a Mac.

However, at this time, it doesn't appear that the project has managed to get the Linux element running on the Mac hardware directly.

The current requirements include an arm64 Linux host with at least 16GB of memory. A Mac is required for access to Xcode, for the creation of the system disk and to build GPU parts of the software.

It also needs a macOS installation supplied by the user, since the project does not distribute Apple's binaries.

Operating system projects

XNULinux is an unusual project, and it is the latest in a series of similar operating system projects using Apple's hardware and software in different ways.

One long-running project is Asahi Linux, which is working to get Linux running natively on Apple Silicon Macs. On October 4, there were the first signs of basic M4 chip support for the project.

More recently, on November 18, SiliconForest OS surfaced as a combination of XNU and Apple's Darwin, the Unix-like core that Apple uses in its operating systems. That project has the similar aim of natively running Mac apps.

However, unlike XNULinux, SiliconForest has been run on Apple's hardware, albeit only on an M1 13-inch MacBook Pro.

items.title: iPhone 18e rumored to get a redesigned square camera bump
items.content_html:
A new report claims to have seen evidence that shows the iPhone 18e will adopt a new camera bump, and the iPhone Air 2 will add a second camera.

Despite previous reports that the forthcoming iPhone 18e will not get a noticeable overhaul, a new report says that Apple is redesigning the camera bump on the rear. A leaker has shared CAD drawings with Engadget of the new iPhone 18e camera bump, which the report says resembles that of the M5 iPad Pro.

However, the leaker hasn't shared the CAD drawings very far. The publication claims to have seen the drawings, but does not show them.

It does further claim that its unspecified source is familiar with the Apple supply chain. Reportedly, they have previously shared accurate tips on the colors of both the iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro ahead of their launch.

The CAD drawings are said to show that there will be a rounded rectangle, almost a square, camera bump. It's said to measure around 28mm by 35mm.

Apple's updating of the camera bump does not mean, though, that it is changing the camera system from the iPhone 17e. Reportedly it will still be a single rear camera, and the bump will also house a microphone and an LED flash.

Exclusive to the iPhone 18e

This emulating of the iPad Pro camera bump is said to be solely for the iPhone 18e. The same CAD drawings reportedly show the base iPhone 18, and the iPhone Air 2.

At least chiefly backing up a recent leak of dummy units for both models, the drawings are said to show a second camera for the iPhone Air 2. It's previously been expected to be mounted vertically below the current single camera, and to be an ultra-wide one.

According to this new report, the iPhone 18 will keep the same layout as the iPhone 17, but its camera module will increase from 3.45mm to 3.8mm.

The report backpedals a little on the CAD drawings, saying that they may be changed since Apple has some months before the phones are released. However, other reports say that displays for both the iPhone 18e and iPhone Air 2 will enter mass production in January, which suggests the whole design is complete.

items.title: 'Ted Lasso' season 5 renewal has been finally been confirmed
items.content_html:
While all evidence pointed to "Ted Lasso" returning to Apple TV for multiple seasons, Apple has only just confirmed that season 5 is indeed happening.

Following claims that pre-production would begin in January 2027, Apple has confirmed that its hit show Ted Lasso has been renewed for a fifth season. Given the success of the fourth season, which drew nearly 300 million U.S. viewing minutes across two days, it's no surprise we're getting more episodes.

Back in July 2026, Jason Sudeikis, who plays the titular Ted Lasso, said he'd like to see more seasons. The following month, Apple's own Eddy Cue similarly said the series was "certainly good enough for that," and that there were "plenty of stories to go on."

The cast of Ted Lasso also reportedly signed a three-year contract in 2025, so a fifth season was effectively inevitable. No details about the plot of the upcoming season are available, and Apple hasn't announced a premiere or launch date.

As for what might happen once the show ends for good, spin-offs have always been a possibility. One featuring the character Roy Kent was heavily rumored.

items.title: Product(Red) HomePod mini & AirPods Max could be revealed soon
items.content_html:
Apple is finally expected to bring back Product(Red) through the HomePod mini 2 and AirPods Max 2 with special editions of those products on or around December 1.

Apple has been releasing products under the Product(Red) banner since 2006. Special editions of various products like iPhones, cases, and accessories have been sold with a portion of the profits going to finance AIDS programs.

According to a report from Bloomberg, Apple is gearing up to release new Product(Red) hardware in honor of (Red)'s 20th anniversary. The new products will be a red HomePod mini 2 and a set of AirPods Max 2 in silver, but with a red Digital Crown.

It is certain that customers will be disappointed that the AirPods Max would only feature a red Digital Crown, but for those holding out on a new pair, it might be enough of a differentiator. A red HomePod mini 2 could be a big hit during the holiday season.

Product(Red) has appeared in many products over the years, like the iPhone 14 in 2022 and the third-generation iPhone SE that was discontinued in 2025. That iPhone SE was the last iPhone being sold with the color, though some cases and accessories still offered it.

It isn't clear why there was a gap of over two years before Apple reentered the hardware space with Product(Red) products. However, the company never gave up on the initiative fully, as it offers a dedicated website detailing the program and various things like Apple Watch faces that use the color.

December 1 is world AIDS Day and the anniversary of the organization, so Apple is expected to announce the products around that date. They would be the first Product(Red) releases since the Apple Watch Series 9 in 2023.

items.title: Threads for iPad is coming, but when is still anybody's guess
items.content_html: Apparently, Threads has decided there are enough users on the platform to justify an iPad-native app. There's no release date. Better late than never, I guess, and it beats Instagram's 15 year run without an iPad app.
